task.goal: Teach 16 middle-school students to interpret a chart with a truncated vertical axis and explain how it changes a visual claim.
hard_constraints: One 40-minute class, printed charts and a whiteboard; no devices.
Do not require students to disclose grades or personal experiences.
Include an individual transfer question on an unseen chart and a criterion that distinguishes noticing the axis from explaining the effect.
task.available_resources: Teacher can print two contrasting charts per student.
task.expected_result: A timed lesson and check for transferable graph interpretation.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Compare the picture with the numbers
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: students compare two drawings of identical data, isolating the axis baseline as the cause of a changed visual impression. The numerical difference stays constant while the apparent bar-height difference changes.

Preparation: print two charts per student. Chart A shows fictional library loans of 80 and 100, with a vertical axis starting at 70. Chart B, reserved for individual transfer, shows fictional museum attendance of 240 and 260, with an axis starting at 230. Label units and ticks clearly. Prepare a zero-baseline version of Chart A on the whiteboard. Use eight pairs; no personal disclosures are needed.

40-minute lesson: 0–4, students inspect A independently and write the claim its appearance suggests. 4–9, pairs identify values, baseline, absolute difference, and percentage increase relative to 80. 9–16, reveal the whiteboard version and ask what changed and what stayed constant. 16–24, pairs develop an explanation linking the omitted baseline to displayed bar lengths: A displays lengths of 10 and 30 despite values of 80 and 100. 24–30, compare explanations and establish that truncation can emphasize differences without changing the data. 30–38, distribute unseen B for individual work: ‘Someone claims attendance nearly doubled. Evaluate the claim using values and explain how the axis affects its appearance.’ 38–40, collect responses and give a brief correction.

Prerequisites and limits: students need basic subtraction and a working understanding of bar charts; percentage calculations can be modeled. Matching chart dimensions and tick spacing matters. Students may overgeneralize that every truncated axis is dishonest; explain that the issue is whether the visual supports the stated claim.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During minutes 9–12, give eight students a baseline-identification prompt and eight a same-data comparison prompt before the common discussion. Collect one-sentence explanations. Score 0 for incorrect interpretation, 1 for noticing the nonzero baseline alone, and 2 for explaining that shortened displayed lengths exaggerate the relative difference while the values remain unchanged. Apply the same criterion to individual transfer responses, additionally checking whether students reject ‘nearly doubled’ using 240 and 260. The mechanism is weakened if comparison produces only more axis mentions, or if students cannot explain the effect on the unseen chart. This small classroom comparison is diagnostic, not reliable causal evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reconstruct the missing part of the bars
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: students physically reconstruct the omitted numerical interval on paper. Connecting each visible bar to its missing baseline segment makes the distortion a measurable consequence rather than a rule to memorize.

Preparation: print Chart A on the upper half of a sheet, leaving room beneath it. It shows fictional shipments of 45 and 50 boxes, a baseline of 40, and one-centimetre tick spacing for five boxes. Students need ordinary pencils. Print unseen Chart B separately: fictional park visitors of 180 and 200, with a baseline of 160. Keep B undistributed until the transfer task.

40-minute lesson: 0–5, students independently describe the apparent comparison in A. 5–10, model reading ticks and distinguishing a bar’s numerical value from its visible length. 10–20, students work individually, then check in eight pairs: extend the axis downward to zero at the same scale and continue both bars into the blank area. Their reconstructed bars should represent 45 and 50, rather than visible lengths representing 5 and 10. 20–27, use the whiteboard to compare the original visible-length ratio of 2 with the actual value ratio of about 1.11. A verbal explanation is acceptable without ratio notation. 27–31, pairs complete: ‘The drawing suggests ___ because ___; the values support ___.’ 31–38, students individually interpret unseen B and evaluate ‘The second park had twice as many visitors.’ 38–40, collect and clarify.

Prerequisites and limits: students must read a uniform scale and extend it with reasonable accuracy. The page needs eight centimetres below A’s baseline; check print sizing beforehand. Drawing accuracy should not determine the interpretation score. This method particularly suits bars whose lengths encode values; it should not be taught as a universal requirement that every graph start at zero.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before reconstruction, collect a brief explanation after students receive the simple instruction ‘Check where the axis begins.’ Compare that response with their post-reconstruction explanation and unseen transfer answer. Use three levels: 0, incorrect; 1, identifies the truncated axis; 2, explains that removing an equal baseline amount makes the displayed bar lengths proportionally farther apart, while the numerical difference is unchanged. Require transfer answers to use 180 and 200 to reject doubling. Reconstruction fails its practical test if students draw correctly but still equate visible-length ratios with value ratios. Improvement over the initial axis-check response is suggestive only, because practice and instruction also contribute.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Audit a claim through competing explanations
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: students adjudicate competing explanations and repair a misleading claim. Requiring a causal warrant between chart design and wording turns axis inspection into an argument about what the evidence supports.

Preparation: print Chart A showing fictional factory output rising from 90 to 100 units, with its vertical axis starting at 80. Include the headline ‘Output doubled!’ and three proposed responses: ‘Correct: the second bar is twice as tall’; ‘Incorrect: the axis starts at 80’; and ‘Incorrect: output rose by 10 units, while the omitted baseline makes the displayed lengths 10 and 20.’ Print unseen Chart B separately, showing fictional ticket sales rising from 300 to 330 with an axis starting at 290. No devices or additional materials beyond pencils and the whiteboard are required.

40-minute lesson: 0–5, students independently select and justify a response to A. 5–13, four groups of four assign roles: value reader, scale checker, claim checker, and explanation editor. Each group must explain why merely naming the baseline leaves the argument incomplete. 13–21, groups present their strongest explanation; the teacher records ‘claim → numerical evidence → visual mechanism’ on the whiteboard. 21–28, groups repair the headline and write an explanation suitable for a younger reader. 28–31, each student independently completes a short explanation without copying the board. 31–38, distribute unseen B: ‘Evaluate “Sales quadrupled.” State the actual change and explain why the chart might suggest that claim.’ 38–40, collect responses and clarify.

Prerequisites and limits: students need subtraction and basic multiplicative comparisons. Explain those comparisons if necessary. Supplied explanations lower the initial writing burden but create a risk of phrase copying, so the individual unseen task is essential. Accept accurate claims that acknowledge increased sales while rejecting the exaggerated magnitude.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the initial independent response as the simple comparator: can students explain the effect after ordinary chart inspection, before group adjudication? Compare it with their independent unseen answer. Score 0 for accepting the unsupported claim or misreading values; 1 for noticing the 290 baseline without explaining its consequence; and 2 for linking visible lengths of 10 and 40 to an exaggerated impression, while recognizing the actual increase of 30 from 300. Equivalent plain-language explanations earn level 2. The mechanism is challenged if students select the supplied strong explanation but produce only ‘the axis is misleading’ on transfer. This checks usable learning, although it cannot isolate the effect of group roles from discussion or repeated practice.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Design an exaggeration, then explain its limits
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: students solve an inverse design problem: choose an axis baseline that makes a fixed increase appear to double. Having to produce the visual effect requires connecting the baseline to displayed bar lengths, rather than merely remembering to inspect an axis.

Preparation: print two charts per student. Chart A is a bar-chart template with fictional deliveries of 60 and 80 boxes stated above it, equal-width bars outlined, and vertical-axis labels left blank. Chart B, kept unseen until assessment, shows fictional attendance of 150 and 180, with a clearly labeled vertical axis starting at 140. Students use ordinary pencils; the teacher uses the whiteboard.

40-minute lesson: 0–5, put a quick baseline-check question on the board: ‘Values are 40 and 50; the axis starts at 30. Does naming the starting point explain the visual effect?’ Collect individual one-sentence answers. 5–10, model that visible bar length represents value minus the baseline, using a separate numerical example. 10–21, eight pairs use Chart A to meet this design brief: ‘Keep 60 and 80 accurate, but choose a baseline so the second visible bar is twice as long.’ Students label the template and explain their choice. A baseline of 40 produces displayed lengths representing 20 and 40. 21–28, pairs explain why their picture suggests doubling although the values do not; verify the arithmetic on the board. 28–31, establish that axis choices can emphasize differences and must be interpreted alongside values. 31–38, students individually answer unseen Chart B: ‘A headline says attendance quadrupled. Evaluate it using the values and explain how the chart could create that impression.’ 38–40, collect and clarify.

Prerequisites and limits: students need subtraction and basic doubling; trial and adjustment are acceptable. Teacher support may be needed for labeling. This applies specifically to bar-length comparisons and does not establish that every truncated axis is inappropriate.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the initial baseline-check response with individual transfer explanations. Score 0 for incorrect interpretation, 1 for identifying the nonzero baseline alone, and 2 for explaining that subtracting the baseline makes displayed lengths proportionally more different while values remain unchanged. Transfer success also requires rejecting quadrupling using 150 and 180; displayed lengths represent 10 and 40. The smallest falsifying check is whether students who successfully design Chart A still give only baseline mentions or accept quadrupling on B. That would undermine the proposed learning mechanism. Improvement is classroom diagnostic evidence, not a causal estimate, because instruction, practice, and chart difficulty also differ.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Commit to a numerical judgment before seeing the picture
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: students establish a numerical anchor before viewing a chart, then use a mismatch between that judgment and the visual impression as a signal to investigate the axis. The intended learning is a reusable reading routine: determine the change from the labels, inspect the scale, and explain any exaggerated impression.

Preparation: print two charts per student. Practice Chart A shows fictional production rising from 100 to 110 items, with a vertical axis starting at 95. Place a small table containing the same values above the chart; folding the sheet hides the chart while leaving the table visible. Reserve Chart B for transfer: fictional admissions rising from 600 to 660, with an axis starting at 580. Label ticks and units clearly. Students need pencils; the teacher uses the whiteboard.

40-minute lesson: 0–6, eight students inspect A’s table first and privately record whether production approximately tripled, then unfold the chart. The other eight inspect the complete sheet immediately. All write a judgment and explanation. 6–12, everyone calculates the actual increase: 10 items, or 10%. 12–20, examine why the picture can suggest tripling: the visible bar lengths represent 5 and 15 above the baseline, although the values are 100 and 110. 20–27, eight pairs rehearse the reading routine on A, with each partner explaining the mismatch aloud. 27–31, students independently write a three-step reminder in their own words. 31–38, distribute unseen B without a table or folding: ‘Evaluate “Admissions quadrupled.” Explain what the values support and how the axis affects the impression.’ 38–40, collect and clarify.

Assumptions and limits: students can subtract and understand doubling; percentage calculation can be modeled. No personal information is requested. Numerical anchoring may improve caution without producing causal understanding, so correct claim rejection alone is insufficient evidence of success.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the initial explanations from the table-first and ordinary-view groups. Score 0 for an incorrect interpretation, 1 for identifying the nonzero baseline without its effect, and 2 for explaining how truncation exaggerates the apparent proportional change while preserving the values. Apply the same distinction to transfer, also requiring rejection of quadrupling using 600 and 660; visible lengths represent 20 and 80. The mechanism is challenged if table-first students merely reject the claim more often but cannot explain the effect, or if students fail without the supplied table. Sixteen students provide a practical diagnostic, not reliable causal evidence.

EXPAND.title: Design a chart to produce a specified impression
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: students become chart designers tasked with making a modest increase look dramatic. Choosing the baseline themselves exposes how the visual impression can change without changing the values. The learning target is explaining that intervention, rather than simply spotting a suspicious axis.

Preparation: print Chart A showing fictional deliveries of 60 and 66 boxes, with a zero baseline and clearly labeled ticks. Leave space beside it for a rough sketch. Reserve printed Chart B for transfer: fictional attendance of 420 and 450, with a baseline of 410. Students use ordinary pencils; the teacher needs only the whiteboard.

40-minute lesson: 0–5, students read A independently and state the actual increase. 5–9, model how to label a uniform vertical scale. 9–18, eight pairs receive a design challenge: ‘Keep the values, labels, units, and chart dimensions fixed. Change the starting value of the vertical axis to make the increase look especially large.’ Students sketch their designs; precision is unnecessary. 18–25, pairs explain their choices. The teacher illustrates a baseline of 54: visible lengths represent 6 and 12, although deliveries did not double. 25–30, students independently finish: ‘Our baseline changes the impression because …; the data still show …’. Discuss why a dramatic appearance cannot establish a dramatic proportional increase. 30–38, distribute unseen B individually: ‘Someone says attendance increased fourfold. Evaluate this claim using the values and explain how the axis encourages that impression.’ 38–40, collect answers and clarify.

Prerequisites and limits: students need subtraction and basic understanding of doubling. Model multiplicative language if necessary. The design constraints must remain fixed so students cannot achieve the effect by changing data. This activity addresses bar lengths; it does not establish that all truncated axes are inappropriate.
EXPAND.experiment: Use students’ initial explanations after inspecting A as the simple comparator. Assess their later individual transfer answers: 0 = incorrect values or acceptance of fourfold growth; 1 = notices the 410 baseline but gives no effect; 2 = correctly rejects fourfold growth using 420 and 450 and explains that omitting the lower portion makes the displayed lengths of 10 and 40 exaggerate the proportional increase. Equivalent plain language earns full credit. The mechanism is challenged if students successfully design dramatic bars but cannot explain the unseen chart. Improvement would be classroom evidence of learning, not proof that design caused it.

EXPAND.title: Learn when an axis observation actually matters
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: students practice discriminating between claims that remain supported and claims whose apparent support comes from truncated bar lengths. Alternating supported and unsupported statements prevents the shortcut ‘nonzero axis means every claim is wrong’ and directs attention to the relationship between a visual encoding and a particular claim.

Preparation: print Chart A showing fictional production of 72 and 80 items, with its vertical axis starting at 64. Print unseen Chart B showing fictional ticket sales of 150 and 165, starting at 145. Put four statements about A on the whiteboard: ‘Production increased’; ‘Production increased by eight items’; ‘Production doubled’; and ‘The visible second bar is twice as long.’ No other printed materials are needed.

40-minute lesson: 0–5, students independently read A and record its values and baseline. 5–12, eight pairs classify each board statement as supported or unsupported, explaining their decisions. 12–20, discuss why three statements are supported but ‘Production doubled’ is not. Distinguish a statement about the drawing from a statement about the quantities represented. Visible lengths represent 8 and 16; the values are 72 and 80. 20–27, the teacher orally offers additional statements about the same chart, alternating numerical claims and appearance claims. Students decide independently before discussing with partners. 27–31, each student writes a rule for checking whether a headline describes the values or mistakenly treats displayed lengths as values. 31–38, distribute unseen B: ‘Evaluate “Ticket sales tripled.” Give the actual increase and explain why the chart could suggest tripling.’ 38–40, collect responses and correct the key confusion.

Prerequisites and limits: students need subtraction and simple multiplicative comparisons. Classification must always require reasons; otherwise students may guess. This approach targets claim discrimination rather than teaching a blanket rule about acceptable baselines. Whether students generalize beyond bar charts remains uncertain.
EXPAND.experiment: Before discussion, retain each student’s initial classifications and reasons as a simple inspection comparator. Score the unseen response separately: 0 = incorrect interpretation; 1 = identifies the nonzero baseline without explaining its effect; 2 = uses 150 and 165 to reject tripling and explains that visible lengths of 5 and 20 create an exaggerated impression. Also check whether students correctly observe that this particular drawing suggests fourfold lengths, not precisely tripling. Exact length calculations are optional if the explanation is accurate. The mechanism is challenged if students reject every statement associated with truncation or merely repeat ‘check the axis.’ Initial-to-transfer improvement is suggestive; the different charts and shared discussion prevent a causal conclusion.

EXPAND.title: Read the scale before revealing the bars
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach an attention routine that delays judging bar heights until students have read the scale. Students cover the bars with a hand, identify the vertical-axis starting value and tick interval, then uncover the bars and read their numerical values. They explain the visual impression only after establishing the numerical comparison. The proposed benefit is reducing anchoring on dramatic-looking bars; whether this brief routine improves transfer is uncertain.

Preparation: print two charts per student, with axes positioned so students can cover the bars while leaving tick labels visible. Chart A shows fictional deliveries of 84 and 96 boxes, starting at 72. Reserve unseen Chart B, showing fictional visitor counts of 210 and 240, starting at 200. Both need clear, uniform ticks and labeled values. Ordinary pencils and the whiteboard suffice.

40-minute lesson: 0–4, introduce the distinction between a visual impression and a numerical claim. 4–10, students silently follow one of two instruction blocks printed on Chart A, as described in the experiment. 10–17, model the scale-first routine for everyone. For A, the visible lengths represent 12 and 24, although 96 is not twice 84. Explain that removing an equal baseline interval makes the displayed length ratio larger than the value ratio. 17–25, eight pairs alternate guiding the routine and explaining its purpose. 25–29, students independently write a causal explanation. 29–37, distribute unseen B: ‘Evaluate the headline “Visitor numbers quadrupled.” State the actual change and explain how the axis could encourage that impression.’ 37–40, collect responses and clarify.

Prerequisites and limits: students must read uniform scales and subtract. No personal disclosures are required. Covering must leave the axis visible. The routine addresses bars encoding quantities by length; students should not infer that every truncated axis invalidates every claim.
EXPAND.experiment: For the initial six-minute activity, randomly give eight students scale-first instructions and eight the simple comparator: ‘Read the chart carefully and evaluate “Deliveries doubled,” explaining your answer.’ Both groups answer the same question independently before discussion. Score responses without reference to assignment: 0 = incorrect or absent interpretation; 1 = notices the nonzero baseline but does not explain its effect; 2 = correctly rejects doubling using values and explains that truncation makes visible lengths 12 and 24, exaggerating the proportional increase. The smallest check is whether more scale-first students earn 2; equal or worse performance provides no support for the proposed immediate benefit. After everyone receives instruction, score unseen B with the same distinction: noticing 200 alone earns 1; explaining that displayed lengths of 10 and 40 suggest quadrupling while actual counts rise by 30 earns 2. Sixteen students provide a classroom diagnostic, not a reliable causal estimate.

Does naming the starting point explain the visual effect?’ Collect individual one-sentence answers. 5–10, model that visible bar length represents value minus the baseline, using a separate numerical example. 10–21, eight pairs use Chart A to meet this design brief: ‘Keep 60 and 80 accurate, but choose a baseline so the second visible bar is twice as long.’ Students label the template and explain their choice. A baseline of 40 produces displayed lengths representing 20 and 40. 21–28, pairs explain why their picture suggests doubling although the values do not; verify the arithmetic on the board. 28–31, establish that axis choices can emphasize differences and must be interpreted alongside values. 31–38, students individually answer unseen Chart B: ‘A headline says attendance quadrupled. Evaluate it using the values and explain how the chart could create that impression.’ 38–40, collect and clarify.

Prerequisites and limits: students need subtraction and basic doubling; trial and adjustment are acceptable. Teacher support may be needed for labeling. This applies specifically to bar-length comparisons and does not establish that every truncated axis is inappropriate.
REFINE.experiment: Compare the initial baseline-check response with individual transfer explanations. Score 0 for incorrect interpretation, 1 for identifying the nonzero baseline alone, and 2 for explaining that subtracting the baseline makes displayed lengths proportionally more different while values remain unchanged. Transfer success also requires rejecting quadrupling using 150 and 180; displayed lengths represent 10 and 40. The smallest falsifying check is whether students who successfully design Chart A still give only baseline mentions or accept quadrupling on B. That would undermine the proposed learning mechanism. Improvement is classroom diagnostic evidence, not a causal estimate, because instruction, practice, and chart difficulty also differ.

REFINE.title: Align the transfer claim with the visual distortion
REFINE.proposal:
Repair candidate 0, the strongest fit because comparing identical data under different baselines makes the visual effect concrete within the available time and materials. Exact weakness: transfer Chart B starts at 230, so values of 240 and 260 produce visible lengths of 10 and 30—a threefold comparison—while the headline claims attendance nearly doubled. This mismatch weakens the check of whether students can explain that particular visual claim. Change only B’s baseline to 220: its visible lengths now represent 20 and 40, directly suggesting doubling despite an actual increase of 20.

Print two charts per student: A, fictional library loans of 80 and 100 with a baseline of 70; and unseen B, fictional museum attendance of 240 and 260 with a baseline of 220. Clearly label axes, units, and uniform ticks. Reserve B until assessment. Prepare a zero-baseline version of A on the whiteboard.

Timing: 0–4 minutes, individually describe A’s apparent comparison; 4–9, eight pairs identify values, baseline, and numerical increase; 9–16, compare A with the whiteboard version, identifying what changed and what stayed constant; 16–24, explain why visible lengths of 10 and 30 exaggerate the relative difference between 80 and 100; 24–30, share and refine explanations; 30–38, individually answer unseen B: ‘Evaluate “Attendance nearly doubled.” Use the values and explain how the axis could create that impression’; 38–40, collect answers and clarify.

Prerequisites: reading uniform bar-chart scales, subtraction, and understanding doubling; percentages are optional. No grades or personal experiences are requested. Remaining limit: this teaches interpretation of bar lengths and should not become a blanket rule against truncated axes in every chart type.
REFINE.experiment: Smallest falsifying check: score the individual B response separately for claim evaluation and visual explanation. Correct evaluation rejects nearly doubling because 260 is only 20 above 240, whereas doubling would be 480. Explanation scores: 0, incorrect or absent; 1, notices the axis starts at 220 but gives no consequence; 2, explains that removing the first 220 makes the visible bars represent 20 and 40, suggesting doubling although the actual values do not double. Equivalent plain language earns 2. Students who identify 220 and reject the headline but cannot explain the apparent doubling have not demonstrated the intended transfer. This is a classroom learning check, not a causal test of the lesson’s effectiveness.

SAVE.title: Compare the picture with the numbers
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: students compare two drawings of identical data, isolating the axis baseline as the cause of a changed visual impression. The numerical difference stays constant while the apparent bar-height difference changes.

Preparation: print two charts per student. Chart A shows fictional library loans of 80 and 100, with a vertical axis starting at 70. Chart B, reserved for individual transfer, shows fictional museum attendance of 240 and 260, with an axis starting at 230. Label units and ticks clearly. Prepare a zero-baseline version of Chart A on the whiteboard. Use eight pairs; no personal disclosures are needed.

40-minute lesson: 0–4, students inspect A independently and write the claim its appearance suggests. 4–9, pairs identify values, baseline, absolute difference, and percentage increase relative to 80. 9–16, reveal the whiteboard version and ask what changed and what stayed constant. 16–24, pairs develop an explanation linking the omitted baseline to displayed bar lengths: A displays lengths of 10 and 30 despite values of 80 and 100. 24–30, compare explanations and establish that truncation can emphasize differences without changing the data. 30–38, distribute unseen B for individual work: ‘Someone claims attendance nearly doubled. Evaluate the claim using values and explain how the axis affects its appearance.’ 38–40, collect responses and give a brief correction.

Prerequisites and limits: students need basic subtraction and a working understanding of bar charts; percentage calculations can be modeled. Matching chart dimensions and tick spacing matters. Students may overgeneralize that every truncated axis is dishonest; explain that the issue is whether the visual supports the stated claim.
SAVE.experiment: During minutes 9–12, give eight students a baseline-identification prompt and eight a same-data comparison prompt before the common discussion. Collect one-sentence explanations. Score 0 for incorrect interpretation, 1 for noticing the nonzero baseline alone, and 2 for explaining that shortened displayed lengths exaggerate the relative difference while the values remain unchanged. Apply the same criterion to individual transfer responses, additionally checking whether students reject ‘nearly doubled’ using 240 and 260. The mechanism is weakened if comparison produces only more axis mentions, or if students cannot explain the effect on the unseen chart. This small classroom comparison is diagnostic, not reliable causal evidence.

SAVE.title: Reconstruct the missing part of the bars
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: students physically reconstruct the omitted numerical interval on paper. Connecting each visible bar to its missing baseline segment makes the distortion a measurable consequence rather than a rule to memorize.

Preparation: print Chart A on the upper half of a sheet, leaving room beneath it. It shows fictional shipments of 45 and 50 boxes, a baseline of 40, and one-centimetre tick spacing for five boxes. Students need ordinary pencils. Print unseen Chart B separately: fictional park visitors of 180 and 200, with a baseline of 160. Keep B undistributed until the transfer task.

40-minute lesson: 0–5, students independently describe the apparent comparison in A. 5–10, model reading ticks and distinguishing a bar’s numerical value from its visible length. 10–20, students work individually, then check in eight pairs: extend the axis downward to zero at the same scale and continue both bars into the blank area. Their reconstructed bars should represent 45 and 50, rather than visible lengths representing 5 and 10. 20–27, use the whiteboard to compare the original visible-length ratio of 2 with the actual value ratio of about 1.11. A verbal explanation is acceptable without ratio notation. 27–31, pairs complete: ‘The drawing suggests ___ because ___; the values support ___.’ 31–38, students individually interpret unseen B and evaluate ‘The second park had twice as many visitors.’ 38–40, collect and clarify.

Prerequisites and limits: students must read a uniform scale and extend it with reasonable accuracy. The page needs eight centimetres below A’s baseline; check print sizing beforehand. Drawing accuracy should not determine the interpretation score. This method particularly suits bars whose lengths encode values; it should not be taught as a universal requirement that every graph start at zero.
SAVE.experiment: Before reconstruction, collect a brief explanation after students receive the simple instruction ‘Check where the axis begins.’ Compare that response with their post-reconstruction explanation and unseen transfer answer. Use three levels: 0, incorrect; 1, identifies the truncated axis; 2, explains that removing an equal baseline amount makes the displayed bar lengths proportionally farther apart, while the numerical difference is unchanged. Require transfer answers to use 180 and 200 to reject doubling. Reconstruction fails its practical test if students draw correctly but still equate visible-length ratios with value ratios. Improvement over the initial axis-check response is suggestive only, because practice and instruction also contribute.

SAVE.title: Audit a claim through competing explanations
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: students adjudicate competing explanations and repair a misleading claim. Requiring a causal warrant between chart design and wording turns axis inspection into an argument about what the evidence supports.

Preparation: print Chart A showing fictional factory output rising from 90 to 100 units, with its vertical axis starting at 80. Include the headline ‘Output doubled!’ and three proposed responses: ‘Correct: the second bar is twice as tall’; ‘Incorrect: the axis starts at 80’; and ‘Incorrect: output rose by 10 units, while the omitted baseline makes the displayed lengths 10 and 20.’ Print unseen Chart B separately, showing fictional ticket sales rising from 300 to 330 with an axis starting at 290. No devices or additional materials beyond pencils and the whiteboard are required.

40-minute lesson: 0–5, students independently select and justify a response to A. 5–13, four groups of four assign roles: value reader, scale checker, claim checker, and explanation editor. Each group must explain why merely naming the baseline leaves the argument incomplete. 13–21, groups present their strongest explanation; the teacher records ‘claim → numerical evidence → visual mechanism’ on the whiteboard. 21–28, groups repair the headline and write an explanation suitable for a younger reader. 28–31, each student independently completes a short explanation without copying the board. 31–38, distribute unseen B: ‘Evaluate “Sales quadrupled.” State the actual change and explain why the chart might suggest that claim.’ 38–40, collect responses and clarify.

Prerequisites and limits: students need subtraction and basic multiplicative comparisons. Explain those comparisons if necessary. Supplied explanations lower the initial writing burden but create a risk of phrase copying, so the individual unseen task is essential. Accept accurate claims that acknowledge increased sales while rejecting the exaggerated magnitude.
SAVE.experiment: Use the initial independent response as the simple comparator: can students explain the effect after ordinary chart inspection, before group adjudication? Compare it with their independent unseen answer. Score 0 for accepting the unsupported claim or misreading values; 1 for noticing the 290 baseline without explaining its consequence; and 2 for linking visible lengths of 10 and 40 to an exaggerated impression, while recognizing the actual increase of 30 from 300. Equivalent plain-language explanations earn level 2. The mechanism is challenged if students select the supplied strong explanation but produce only ‘the axis is misleading’ on transfer. This checks usable learning, although it cannot isolate the effect of group roles from discussion or repeated practice.

SAVE.title: Design a chart to produce a specified impression
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: students become chart designers tasked with making a modest increase look dramatic. Choosing the baseline themselves exposes how the visual impression can change without changing the values. The learning target is explaining that intervention, rather than simply spotting a suspicious axis.

Preparation: print Chart A showing fictional deliveries of 60 and 66 boxes, with a zero baseline and clearly labeled ticks. Leave space beside it for a rough sketch. Reserve printed Chart B for transfer: fictional attendance of 420 and 450, with a baseline of 410. Students use ordinary pencils; the teacher needs only the whiteboard.

40-minute lesson: 0–5, students read A independently and state the actual increase. 5–9, model how to label a uniform vertical scale. 9–18, eight pairs receive a design challenge: ‘Keep the values, labels, units, and chart dimensions fixed. Change the starting value of the vertical axis to make the increase look especially large.’ Students sketch their designs; precision is unnecessary. 18–25, pairs explain their choices. The teacher illustrates a baseline of 54: visible lengths represent 6 and 12, although deliveries did not double. 25–30, students independently finish: ‘Our baseline changes the impression because …; the data still show …’. Discuss why a dramatic appearance cannot establish a dramatic proportional increase. 30–38, distribute unseen B individually: ‘Someone says attendance increased fourfold. Evaluate this claim using the values and explain how the axis encourages that impression.’ 38–40, collect answers and clarify.

Prerequisites and limits: students need subtraction and basic understanding of doubling. Model multiplicative language if necessary. The design constraints must remain fixed so students cannot achieve the effect by changing data. This activity addresses bar lengths; it does not establish that all truncated axes are inappropriate.
SAVE.experiment: Use students’ initial explanations after inspecting A as the simple comparator. Assess their later individual transfer answers: 0 = incorrect values or acceptance of fourfold growth; 1 = notices the 410 baseline but gives no effect; 2 = correctly rejects fourfold growth using 420 and 450 and explains that omitting the lower portion makes the displayed lengths of 10 and 40 exaggerate the proportional increase. Equivalent plain language earns full credit. The mechanism is challenged if students successfully design dramatic bars but cannot explain the unseen chart. Improvement would be classroom evidence of learning, not proof that design caused it.

SAVE.title: Learn when an axis observation actually matters
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: students practice discriminating between claims that remain supported and claims whose apparent support comes from truncated bar lengths. Alternating supported and unsupported statements prevents the shortcut ‘nonzero axis means every claim is wrong’ and directs attention to the relationship between a visual encoding and a particular claim.

Preparation: print Chart A showing fictional production of 72 and 80 items, with its vertical axis starting at 64. Print unseen Chart B showing fictional ticket sales of 150 and 165, starting at 145. Put four statements about A on the whiteboard: ‘Production increased’; ‘Production increased by eight items’; ‘Production doubled’; and ‘The visible second bar is twice as long.’ No other printed materials are needed.

40-minute lesson: 0–5, students independently read A and record its values and baseline. 5–12, eight pairs classify each board statement as supported or unsupported, explaining their decisions. 12–20, discuss why three statements are supported but ‘Production doubled’ is not. Distinguish a statement about the drawing from a statement about the quantities represented. Visible lengths represent 8 and 16; the values are 72 and 80. 20–27, the teacher orally offers additional statements about the same chart, alternating numerical claims and appearance claims. Students decide independently before discussing with partners. 27–31, each student writes a rule for checking whether a headline describes the values or mistakenly treats displayed lengths as values. 31–38, distribute unseen B: ‘Evaluate “Ticket sales tripled.” Give the actual increase and explain why the chart could suggest tripling.’ 38–40, collect responses and correct the key confusion.

Prerequisites and limits: students need subtraction and simple multiplicative comparisons. Classification must always require reasons; otherwise students may guess. This approach targets claim discrimination rather than teaching a blanket rule about acceptable baselines. Whether students generalize beyond bar charts remains uncertain.
SAVE.experiment: Before discussion, retain each student’s initial classifications and reasons as a simple inspection comparator. Score the unseen response separately: 0 = incorrect interpretation; 1 = identifies the nonzero baseline without explaining its effect; 2 = uses 150 and 165 to reject tripling and explains that visible lengths of 5 and 20 create an exaggerated impression. Also check whether students correctly observe that this particular drawing suggests fourfold lengths, not precisely tripling. Exact length calculations are optional if the explanation is accurate. The mechanism is challenged if students reject every statement associated with truncation or merely repeat ‘check the axis.’ Initial-to-transfer improvement is suggestive; the different charts and shared discussion prevent a causal conclusion.
